To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
two genes, tomosyn‐ 1 and ‐2 encode seven splice variants of tomosyn in the mammalian nervous system.
two genes encode seven tomosyn splice variants, which are differentially expressed in the developing brain, and share a conserved structure, including a unique hypervariable domain.
two distinct genes encode seven isoforms of the syntaxin‐binding tomosyn protein, which share a conserved structure, including SNARE domains, but differ in the hypervariable domain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and functional analysis of a novel protein family.
the expression and regulation of the tomosyn family of proteins.
the molecular and cellular characterization of the tomosyn gene family.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tomosyn is a protein with a unique variable region and conserved SNARE domain and WD40 repeats.
the mammalian brain expresses seven tomosyn‐related proteins, all of which are composed of a hypervarible domain, a SNARE‐binding domain and WD40 domains.
tomosyn is a family of proteins, which is composed of two genes and seven isoforms, and that these isoforms share a conserved structure and a unique variable domain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tomosyn is not only an interesting regulator of neuronal secretion, but also a good model for the analysis of gene duplication and evolution in the mammalian nervous system.
tomosyn isoform composition changes during development in a region‐specific manner, and that tomosyns may have different functions in the nervous system.
tomosyns represent a family of WD40‐containing proteins that are involved in the control of SNARE‐mediated secretion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of tomosyn isoform genes is tightly regulated during development.
the mammalian brain expresses two distinct genes that encode seven tomosyn‐related proteins.
tomosyn expression is developmentally regulated and is not restricted to a single isoform.
